items.title: A reformulation of the t-test in single-cell transcriptomics dramatically reduces false positives
items.by: Kviman, O.; Ferreira, P. F.; Jun, S.-H.; Toosi, H.; Lagergren, J.
items.why: A statistical-methods preprint on false positives in the default differential-expression tests used for single-cell cluster annotation. It is a bioRxiv preprint and not peer reviewed; the abstract's claims rest on the authors' own theoretical and empirical work, and the code is linked on GitHub.
items.takeaway: The authors say default single-cell t-tests inflate false positives and propose LN's t-test, which they say keeps the speed.

items.title: Lessons in Bemistry: identifying the signature of a medicinal chemist
items.why: A short critical read on shortcut learning in molecular ML. It asks whether activity benchmarks can be solved by inferring who made a molecule, and it states its own limits, such as the lack of balanced accuracy.
items.takeaway: The underlying preprint reports predicting the medicinal chemist from structure alone (top-1 27%, top-5 60%). The post flags that unbalanced author counts may inflate this.

items.title: Identifying Interactions at Scale for LLMs
items.why: Interpretability through ablation, extended to interactions between features, training examples and attention heads. The results are the authors' own.
items.takeaway: The method relies on sparsity, low-degree interactions and, for ProxySPEX, hierarchy. The authors say this cuts the ablations needed by about 10x.

items.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
items.why: A thorough, code-backed walkthrough of how LLMs encode token position, from learned absolute embeddings through sinusoidal encodings to RoPE.
items.takeaway: Even a causal mask gives implicit order information, but explicit positional methods still give attention a direct signal about position.

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.why: A careful survey of how scaling laws are fitted, covering Kaplan, Chinchilla's three methods, how the two are reconciled, and the data-limited regime. It is useful for judging scaling claims critically.
items.takeaway: Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla disagree on compute-optimal allocation, and the post covers why fitting these laws is tricky.

items.title: AlphaFold2 @ CASP14: “It feels like one’s child has left home.”
items.why: A first-hand expert assessment of AlphaFold2 at CASP14 that separates the quantitative advance from the loose claim that protein folding is solved. It is a 2020 opinion piece and its forecasts are speculative.
items.takeaway: The author reports a median GDT_TS of 92.4. He also notes the caveat that AF2 is trained on PDB structures and so predicts crystal-like structures.

items.title: A Recipe for Cells
items.why: A quantitative inventory of what an E. coli cell is made of and what it costs to build, framed around why cells are hard to recreate from parts. It adds cell-biology breadth with concrete numbers.
items.takeaway: The essay argues that a list of ingredients is not a recipe: noise and fault tolerance are what make cells hard to rebuild.

items.title: Rotary position embedding (RoPE)
items.why: Rotate query and key vectors to make attention sensitive to relative position. A worked mathematical explanation of RoPE.

items.title: Exponential generating functions (EGF)
items.why: Encode a sequence with factorial-weighted coefficients. Explore why this representation is useful for counting labelled structures.

earlier.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
earlier.why: This preprint gives an open recipe for turning pretrained image generators into multi-task perception systems. It reports ablations on design choices and says it releases code and checkpoints. The benchmark gains are the authors' own and unreplicated.
earlier.takeaway: The authors report that individually helpful design choices can hurt when combined.

earlier.title: High-Low Frequency Detectors
earlier.why: A Colah-era Circuits article that uses feature visualization, dataset examples, tuning curves and weight analysis to explain how a family of vision-model neurons works. It is a rigorous example of mechanistic interpretability reasoning.
earlier.takeaway: The authors find 15 neurons in InceptionV1's mixed3a layer that detect high-to-low spatial-frequency transitions. They argue these are built from the same two upstream clusters arranged in different spatial layouts.
